sections.text: npm install -D spana-test @varar/varar @varar/vitest @varar/cli vitest vite Your package.json must have "type": "module" .

sections.heading: Configure
sections.text: title="varar.config.json" { "docs": { "include": ["varar/ / .md"], "exclude": [] }, "steps": ["src/varar/ / .steps.ts"] } title="vitest.config.ts" plugins: [vararPlugin()], test: { testTimeout: 30 000, reporters: ["default", new VararResultsReporter()] }, }); The Varar plugin replaces Vitest's test.include with the docs.include list.

sections.heading: Write the spec
sections.text: title="varar/cart.md" Shopping cart A new visitor sees that the cart shows 0 items. When the shopper adds 2 items to the cart, the cart shows 2 items.

sections.heading: Write the steps
sections.text: title="src/varar/cart.steps.ts" let session: Session undefined; afterAll(() = session?.disconnect()); // The state factory runs for each document. Reuse one session, relaunch the app. const { stimulus, sensor } = steps(async () = { session ??= await connect({ platform: "web", baseUrl: "http://localhost:4173" }); await session.launch(); return { app: session }; }); stimulus("the shopper adds {int} items to the cart", async ({ app }, count) = { for (let i = 0; i el.id === testID)?.text; } sensor("the cart shows {int} items", async ({ app }) = Number(await textOf(app, "cart-count"))); Run it: npx vitest run If the app shows a different number, Varar reports the cell that does not match: CellMismatchError: cell 1: expected 3 but was 2

sections.heading: Other platforms
sections.text: Change the connect() options. The steps stay the same, because { testID } selectors work on every platform: await connect({ platform: "android", packageName: "com.example.app" }); await connect({ platform: "ios", bundleId: "com.example.app" }); See connect() options for Electron and Electrobun.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.text: - Runs one session at a time in each Vitest worker. Spana's shared pool and --parallel are not used. - --changed-since , Spana reporters and @web / @ios tags do not apply. Use Vitest's own filters and reporters. - Varar is at version 0.8. Its API can change.

title: CLI Commands
description: Full command and flag reference for the spana CLI.

sections.text: The spana binary is the entry point for running flows, validating projects, inspecting live UI state, and scaffolding new tests.

sections.heading: spana test
sections.text: Run discovered flows or a specific file. spana test [path] [options] path is optional. If omitted, Spana discovers flows from flowDir in spana.config.ts .

sections.heading: Filtering and targeting
sections.text: Flag Description -------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------- --platform Restrict the run to one or more platforms --tag Run only flows with matching tags --grep Run only flows whose names match the pattern --device Run on one specific local device --devices , Run on specific devices in parallel mode

sections.heading: Parallelism and execution control
sections.text: Flag Description --------------------------- -------------------------------------------------- --parallel Auto-discover devices and run flows in parallel --workers Max workers per platform in parallel mode --retries Retry failed flows n times --bail Stop scheduling new flows after n final failures --shard / Run one deterministic CI shard --debug-on-failure Open an interactive REPL on the first failure

sections.heading: Iteration helpers
sections.text: Flag Description ----------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --watch Re-run when flows or config change --changed Run only changed flow files from git --changed-since Run the filters from spana.config.ts against the git diff from . Without filters , it warns and runs all flows --last-failed Re-run only flows that failed in the last run --update-baselines Rewrite screenshot and file-based ARIA snapshot baselines --strict-cache Accepted for replay cache strict mode, but spana test does not use it yet (see Replay Cache)

sections.heading: Output and configuration
sections.text: Flag Description -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ --reporter Comma-separated reporters: console , json , junit , html , allure , github , or a custom module path (default console ) --js-coverage Save JavaScript coverage for Chromium web flows --config Use a non-default config file --validate-config Validate config and exit before discovery --quiet , -q Suppress pass output and show failures plus summary --verbose Print detailed failure diagnostics and hierarchy

sections.heading: Appium and cloud overrides
sections.text: Flag Description -------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------- --driver Override execution.mode --appium-url Override execution.appium.serverUrl --appium-auto-start Spawn a local Appium server in Appium mode (ignores any Appium URL) --caps Load Appium capabilities from JSON --caps-json Inline Appium capabilities JSON --no-provider-reporting Skip BrowserStack/Sauce Labs session result reporting

sections.heading: Examples
sections.text: Run the whole suite spana test Run one file on web spana test flows/login.flow.ts --platform web Run smoke flows on Android and iOS spana test --tag smoke --platform android,ios Run the last failures only spana test --last-failed Re-run automatically while editing flows spana test --watch Parallelize across discovered devices spana test --parallel --workers 2 Pin the run to specific devices spana test --platform android,ios --devices emulator-5554,SIM-1 Refresh screenshot baselines spana test --update-baselines

sections.heading: Framework-app multi-device showcase
sections.text: When you want a concrete local showcase run from this repo, start in packages/spana so the bundled framework demo config and flows resolve directly: Inspect the device IDs you can target spana devices Iterate on one pinned device first spana test ./flows/framework-app --config ./spana.config.ts --platform android --device emulator-5554 Then fan out the same showcase flows across specific Android + iOS targets spana test ./flows/framework-app \ --config ./spana.config.ts \ --platform android,ios \ --devices emulator-5554, \ --parallel \ --workers 1 Use --device when you want one reproducible local target while debugging a flow, then switch to --devices plus --parallel when you want the framework-app demo to showcase the same suite across multiple local devices. CLI flags override spana.config.ts . Filtering happens before sharding, so each shard sees a deterministic slice of the already-filtered flow list.

sections.heading: spana hierarchy
sections.text: Dump the current UI hierarchy from a live session. spana hierarchy [--platform ] [--config path] [--json] [--pretty] --platform defaults to web . Use this to inspect the raw element tree when selectors are not behaving as expected.

sections.heading: spana selectors
sections.text: List actionable elements and suggested selectors for the current screen. spana selectors [--platform ] [--config path] [--json] [--pretty] This command connects to the running app, inspects the hierarchy, and returns the best selectors Spana can infer for each visible element. For deeper examples of both commands, see Agent Commands.

sections.heading: spana validate
sections.text: Validate flow files without connecting to devices. spana validate [path] [--json] path defaults to ./flows . Validation checks that flows load correctly and that project-level flow issues are surfaced before a real run.

sections.heading: spana validate-config
sections.text: Validate spana.config.ts without starting drivers or discovering flows. spana validate-config [path] [--config path] [--json] This is useful in CI or pre-commit hooks when you want a fast config sanity check.

sections.heading: spana doctor
sections.text: Check environment readiness before running tests. spana doctor [options] Flag Description -------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------- --platform Limit diagnostics to selected platforms --config Load a specific config file --driver Force local or Appium diagnostics --appium-url Override the Appium endpoint under test --caps Load Appium capabilities from a file --caps-json Inline Appium capabilities JSON --json Emit machine-readable doctor results --pretty Pretty-print JSON output Use doctor before a new CI environment, after simulator/device setup changes, or when a session fails to start and you want a quick readiness report.

sections.heading: spana studio
sections.text: Launch the Studio UI for recording, inspection, and running flows. spana studio [--config path] [--port 4400] [--no-open] See Studio for the full workflow.

sections.heading: spana init
sections.text: Scaffold a new Spana project. spana init [--preset ] [--force] Only capacitor-web-first writes a preset config without prompts. The other preset names are accepted, but Spana runs the interactive wizard. See Init for the generated config and starter flow.

sections.heading: spana init-flow
sections.text: Generate a starter .flow.ts file. spana init-flow [options] Flag Description ------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------- --platform Add platform tags to the generated flow --tag Add custom tags --preset Start from a built-in flow template (default smoke ) --output Write to a custom file path --force Overwrite an existing file

sections.heading: Examples
sections.text: spana init-flow "checkout smoke" --preset smoke --platform web,android --tag smoke spana init-flow "login auth" --preset auth --output flows/auth/login.flow.ts

sections.heading: spana devices
sections.text: List connected devices and simulators. spana devices [--json] Spana checks web, Android, iOS, Electron, and Electrobun targets. Output includes platform, device name, device type, and connection state. This is the fastest way to confirm the IDs you should pass to --device or --devices .

sections.heading: spana daemon
sections.text: Inspect or stop the warm WDA / UiAutomator2 daemons that Spana has registered (see execution.warmDaemons ). spana daemon [status stop] status (the default) lists each registered daemon with kind, device ID, host, port, and PID. stop stops all of them.

sections.heading: spana mcp
sections.text: Start the stdio MCP server for coding agents. spana mcp See Agent Commands & MCP Server for the tool list.

sections.heading: spana version
sections.text: Print the installed CLI version. spana version

sections.heading: Exit codes
sections.text: Code Meaning ---- ----------------- 0 Command succeeded 1 Command failed

title: Agent Commands & MCP Server
description: Model-free stdio MCP server (spana mcp), Verified Replay Cache, and agent CLI commands (selectors, hierarchy, validate, doctor).

sections.text: spana is built for AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity) with both a model-free stdio MCP server ( spana mcp ) and structured --json CLI commands.

sections.heading: spana mcp (Model-Free Stdio MCP Server)
sections.text: Start Spana's stdio MCP server so any MCP-compatible agent can drive a live Web, iOS, Android, Electron, or Electrobun session and export the recorded steps as a .flow.ts file: { "mcpServers": { "spana": { "command": "npx", "args": ["spana", "mcp"] } } }

sections.heading: Exposed MCP tools
sections.text: The server holds one session at a time. Each action tool that succeeds returns the matching .flow.ts line ( codeLine ) and records it for export. Tool Description ------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ spana session start Connect to a target ( web , android , ios , electron , electrobun ). Options: baseUrl , packageName , bundleId , device , headless (default true ), and cdpUrl (Electron / Electrobun). Replaces any open session spana observe Return actionable elements with suggested selectors (default max 60, set maxElements ), plus the last 15 console logs and last 10 JS errors spana tap Tap an element by { testID } , { text } , or { accessibilityLabel } (add "systemUI": true for OS UI); records app.tap(...) spana input text Type text into the focused control; records app.inputText(...) spana fill Tap the element, then type value ; records app.fill(selector, value) spana open link Open a URL or deep link; records app.openLink(...) spana assert visible Check the current element list once (no auto-wait) for a testID , text , or accessibilityLabel match; records expect(...).toBeVisible() . On a miss, returns up to 20 available test IDs spana assert accessible Record an expect.screen().toBeAccessible(...) line ( standard , failOnSeverity ). On web, it also returns up to 10 unlabeled controls as quickIssues spana assert screenshot Capture a PNG and record an expect.screen().toMatchScreenshot(name, ...) line ( mode , maxDiffPixelRatio ). It does not compare against a baseline The flow expect API has no expect.screen() today, so lines recorded by spana assert accessible and spana assert screenshot must be edited before the exported flow runs. Use expect(selector).toPassAccessibilityAudit() and expect(selector).toMatchScreenshot(name) instead. spana screenshot Return a PNG screenshot of the current screen spana diagnostics Return element and testID counts, the last 25 console logs, and the last 15 JS errors spana export flow Return the recorded steps as a .flow.ts file without disconnecting spana session stop Disconnect and return the generated .flow.ts file spana run flow Run an existing .flow.ts file (optional platform ) and return passed: true/false

sections.heading: Verified Replay Cache (.spana/cache/ & --strict-cache)
sections.text: ReplaySession and ReplayCacheStore (exported from spana-test ) record agentic actions to .spana/cache/ only after a real assertion verifies them. On a cache hit, ReplaySession.act() replays the recorded actions with no LLM call. ReplaySession has three modes: read-write (default: on a miss or mismatch, hand off to the executor and save the healed recording), strict (fail on a missing or mismatched recording), and off . Accepted by the CLI, but not yet passed to the runner spana test --strict-cache Today, spana test accepts --strict-cache and the replayCache config key but does not use them. To get strict mode, create ReplaySession with mode: "strict" in your own code.

sections.heading: spana selectors
sections.text: List all actionable elements on screen with suggested selectors. spana selectors --platform [--config path] [--json] [--pretty] Plain output is a JSON array. With --json , Spana wraps that array in a versioned machine-readable envelope. spana selectors --platform android [ { "suggestedSelector": { "testID": "login-button" }, "elementType": "android.widget.Button", "text": "Sign In", "bounds": { "x": 24, "y": 480, "width": 328, "height": 48 }, "id": "login-button" }, { "suggestedSelector": { "text": "Forgot password?" }, "elementType": "android.widget.TextView", "text": "Forgot password?", "bounds": { "x": 120, "y": 544, "width": 136, "height": 20 } } ] Only visible elements with an id , text , or accessibilityLabel are listed. Fields without a value are left out. suggestedSelector follows priority: testID (from id ) accessibilityLabel text . Feed this output directly to an agent to choose which element to interact with.

sections.heading: Filtering with jq
sections.text: Elements that have a testID spana selectors --platform web jq '.[] select(.id != null)' Just the suggested selectors spana selectors --platform ios jq '[.[].suggestedSelector]'

sections.heading: spana hierarchy
sections.text: Dump the full UI element tree as structured JSON. spana hierarchy --platform [--config path] [--json] [--pretty] Plain output is the raw hierarchy JSON. With --json , Spana wraps it in a versioned machine-readable envelope. spana hierarchy --platform web --pretty { "elementType": "body", "bounds": { "x": 0, "y": 0, "width": 375, "height": 812 }, "children": [ { "elementType": "main", "bounds": { "x": 0, "y": 0, "width": 375, "height": 812 }, "children": [ { "elementType": "textbox", "id": "email-input", "bounds": { "x": 24, "y": 200, "width": 328, "height": 44 } } ] } ] } On web, elementType is the ARIA role, or the HTML tag when there is no role. Each node can have id , text , value , accessibilityLabel , resourceId , elementType , bounds , enabled , visible , clickable , focused , attributes , and children . Use spana hierarchy when spana selectors does not include the element you need, or to understand the structural relationship between elements.

sections.heading: spana validate
sections.text: Validate flow files without a device connection. Catches common mistakes before running tests. spana validate [path] [--json] path defaults to ./flows . Exits 0 if all flows are valid, non-zero if any errors found. Does not execute the flows. Checks performed: - Every flow loads and has a name and fn - No duplicate flow names across files - Platform values are valid ( web , android , ios only) - Flow directory exists and contains flow files spana validate ✓ 5 flow(s) valid spana validate flows/ ✗ flows/login.flow.ts: Duplicate flow name "Login test" (also in flows/auth.flow.ts) ✗ flows/broken.flow.ts: Invalid platform "windows" - must be web, android, or ios ✗ flows/empty.flow.ts: Invalid flow definition: missing name or fn Use spana validate in CI preflight or as part of an agent loop before committing generated flow files.

sections.heading: Agent workflow
sections.text: The typical agent-driven authoring loop: 1. Navigate the app to the screen you want to test, then discover elements spana selectors --platform android jq '.[] select(.id != null)' 2. Generate and write a flow file (done by the agent) 3. Validate the flow without a device spana validate flows/my-new-flow.ts 4. Run the flow and capture JSON results (one JSON event per line) spana test flows/my-new-flow.ts --reporter json 5. Read failures from the JSON events and iterate spana test flows/my-new-flow.ts --reporter json jq -R 'fromjson? select(.event == "flowFail")' This loop requires no manual interaction. spana validate catches structural errors before device time is spent. --reporter json gives the agent machine-readable pass/fail data with error messages. graph LR A[Agent] -- spana selectors B[Discover elements] B -- generate code C[Write flow.ts] C -- spana validate D[Validate schema] D -- spana test --reporter json E[Execute on device] E -- read JSON errors F[Fix and retry] F -- C

sections.heading: Agent skill file
sections.text: spana ships with a ready-made skill file for AI coding agents at .agents/skills/spana-testing/SKILL.md in the repo. It covers element discovery, flow writing patterns, selectors, validation, error handling, and platform-specific notes. To use it with your AI agent: 1. Copy the skill file into your project: mkdir -p .agents/skills/spana-testing cp node modules/spana-test/.agents/skills/spana-testing/SKILL.md .agents/skills/spana-testing/ 2. Or reference it in your CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md : Testing For writing E2E tests, follow the spana testing skill at: .agents/skills/spana-testing/SKILL.md 3. Or point your agent to it directly: Read .agents/skills/spana-testing/SKILL.md and use it to write a test for the login flow. The skill file is self-contained — it includes the full API reference, workflow loop, and common patterns so the agent can start writing tests immediately.

title: Init
description: Scaffold a new spana project with interactive prompts.

sections.text: The spana init command generates a starter config file and example flow through an interactive wizard.

sections.heading: Usage
sections.text: spana init

sections.heading: Options
sections.text: Flag Description ----------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --force Overwrite existing spana.config.ts (and the starter flow) if present --preset local-web , local-react-native , capacitor-web-first , browserstack , or saucelabs Only capacitor-web-first changes the output today: it skips the wizard (see below). The other preset names are accepted, but Spana still runs the interactive wizard.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: The wizard asks: 1. Which platforms to test -- web (Playwright), Android (UiAutomator2), iOS (WebDriverAgent) 2. App details per platform: - Web: app URL (default http://localhost:3000 ) - Android: package name (default com.example.myapp ) - iOS: bundle ID (default com.example.myapp ) Then it creates: File Description ----------------------- ------------------------------------------------ spana.config.ts Config file with your platform and app settings flows/example.flow.ts Starter flow with a smoke test you can customize

sections.heading: Generated config
sections.text: title="spana.config.ts" apps: { web: { url: "http://localhost:3000" }, android: { packageName: "com.example.myapp" }, }, platforms: ["web", "android"], flowDir: "./flows", reporters: ["console"], defaults: { waitTimeout: 5 000, }, });

sections.heading: Generated flow
sections.text: title="flows/example.flow.ts" "Example - app loads successfully", { tags: ["smoke"], platforms: ["web", "android"] }, async ({ app, expect }) = { await expect({ text: "Hello" }).toBeVisible(); }, );

sections.heading: capacitor-web-first preset
sections.text: spana init --preset capacitor-web-first This preset writes files without prompts: File Description ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- spana.config.ts All five targets ( web , android , ios , electron , electrobun ) with execution.bridge and execution.warmDaemons turned on flows/sign-in.flow.ts Sign-in flow that taps a systemUI() OAuth sheet Install spana-bridge in your test builds to use the DOM bridge.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: After running spana init : 1. Install spana: npm install -D spana-test 2. Add spana-output to your .gitignore 3. Edit flows/example.flow.ts with selectors from your app 4. Discover selectors: spana selectors 5. Run tests: spana test

title: Studio
description: Local web UI for interactive element inspection and test management.

sections.text: Spana Studio is a local web interface that bundles an Element Inspector , a Test Runner Dashboard , and a Recorder into a single tool. It lets you visually inspect device screens, explore element trees, record new flows, and run test flows with real-time feedback — all from your browser.

sections.heading: Launching Studio
sections.text: spana studio [options]

sections.heading: Options
sections.text: Flag Description ----------------- -------------------------------------------------- --port Port to serve on (default: 4400 ) --no-open Don't auto-open the browser --config Path to config file (default: ./spana.config.ts ) Start on the default port and open the browser spana studio Use a custom port, skip auto-open spana studio --port 4000 --no-open Point at a non-default config spana studio --config ./config/spana.staging.ts

sections.heading: Element Inspector
sections.text: Studio Inspector Connect to a running device or simulator, then interact with a live screenshot of the current screen. - Tap to inspect — click any element in the screenshot to see its properties (testID, text, accessibility label, bounds). - Element tree — browse the full hierarchy in a sidebar tree view. - Copy selectors — one-click copy of the best selector for any element, ready to paste into a flow file. This gives you the same information as spana selectors and spana hierarchy , but in a visual, point-and-click workflow.

sections.heading: Test Runner Dashboard
sections.text: Studio Test Runner Discover and run flow files without leaving the browser. - Flow discovery — automatically lists all flows found under your configured flowDir . - Device selector — pick the target device, emulator, or simulator for each selected platform from the toolbar. - Run tests — execute one or many flows with real-time progress updates. - Step details — expand any step to see its status, duration, and captured screenshot.

sections.heading: Capture toggles
sections.text: Two checkboxes control screenshot capture during a run: Toggle Behavior ----------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Screenshots Also capture artifacts when a flow passes ( artifacts.captureOnSuccess ) Step captures Capture per-step screenshots ( artifacts.captureSteps ), useful for visual debugging When either toggle is on, failure capture, screenshots, and UI hierarchy dumps are also turned on for that run.

sections.heading: Session persistence
sections.text: Test results persist across tab switches within the same Studio session. You can jump between the Inspector, Runner, and Recorder without losing run history or step details.

sections.heading: Recorder
sections.text: Record a new flow by driving a live web, Android, or iOS session from Studio. - Start Recording — open a recording session for the selected platform and device. - Record actions — click the screenshot to tap, double-tap, long-press, type text, or add an expect(...).toBeVisible() check; use the toolbar for tap, type text, scroll, swipe, and back. Each action runs on the device, and Studio stores the selector and alternative selectors for it. - Delete — remove a recorded action. - Generate / Save — generate flow code from the recorded actions, or save it to / .ts (default flows/ ).

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Studio is an embedded React frontend served directly from the CLI binary — no separate install required. The frontend communicates with the CLI backend through an oRPC API layer, giving you type-safe requests between the browser and device connections.

sections.heading: Development
sections.text: If you're working on Studio itself, run the Vite dev server with hot reload: cd apps/studio bun run dev The Vite dev server runs on port 4401 . The frontend sends its API calls to /rpc on the page's own origin.

title: Reporters
description: Built-in reporters for test output — console, JSON, JUnit, HTML, Allure, and GitHub.

sections.text: Spana ships six reporters. Use one or combine several to get both human-readable output and machine-readable artifacts from the same run.

sections.heading: Enabling reporters
sections.text: CLI flag (comma-separated; if you repeat --reporter , only the last one is used): spana test --reporter console,html Config file ( spana.config.ts ): reporters: ["console", "html"], }); The CLI flag replaces reporters from the config. With neither set, Spana uses console . Multiple reporters run simultaneously. Each receives the same flow results as they complete. ---

sections.heading: Console (default)
sections.text: Human-readable terminal output with pass/fail symbols, per-platform summaries, and failure details. Enable: active by default. Explicitly: --reporter console . Output: stdout. ✓ login flow (1243ms) ✗ [android] login flow (3891ms) web (Playwright) ✓ 1/1 passed (1.2s) android (UiAutomator2) ✗ 0/1 passed (3.9s) --- Failures --- ✗ [android] login flow Category: timeout Timed out waiting for selector "welcome-text" 1/2 passed, 1 failed (3.9s) Flaky tests (passed on retry) are tagged [flaky, passed on attempt N] and listed with in a "Flaky" section. Scenario steps (Given/When/Then) are printed inline when using Gherkin-style flows. When to use: local development and quick CI feedback. ---

sections.heading: JSON
sections.text: Streams newline-delimited JSON events to stdout. Each line is a self-contained JSON object. Enable: --reporter json Output: stdout (one JSON object per line). Each event holds every field of the FlowResult or RunSummary , plus event . Events emitted: Event When ------------- ---------------------------------------------- flowPass A flow finishes successfully flowFail A flow fails runComplete All flows have finished; includes full summary {"event":"flowPass","name":"login flow","platform":"web","status":"passed","durationMs":1243} {"event":"flowFail","name":"login flow","platform":"android","status":"failed","durationMs":3891,"error":{"message":"Timed out","category":"timeout"}} {"event":"runComplete","total":2,"passed":1,"failed":1,"skipped":0,"flaky":0,"durationMs":3891} When to use: piping results into other tools, custom dashboards, or CI scripts that parse structured output. ---

sections.heading: JUnit
sections.text: Generates a JUnit XML file compatible with Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and most CI systems that consume test reports. Enable: --reporter junit Output: /junit-report.xml (default ./spana-output/junit-report.xml ). ... Results are grouped by platform into elements. Scenario steps, driver steps, and attachments are included in when present. When to use: CI pipelines that display JUnit test results (GitHub Actions test-reporter , Jenkins JUnit plugin, GitLab test reports). ---

sections.heading: HTML
sections.text: HTML Report Single-file HTML report with a dark theme, responsive layout, and embedded screenshots (base64-inlined). Enable: --reporter html Output: /report.html (default ./spana-output/report.html ). The report includes: - Summary cards -- passed/total, total time, platform count. - Per-platform sections -- status badge, duration, driver and scenario steps. - Step screenshots -- inline images from each step that captured a screenshot. - Final-state screenshots -- side-by-side comparison of the final screen on each platform. - Failure details -- error messages displayed inline. - Video and playback -- when artifacts.video is "on" or "retain-on-failure" , a video player for the flow recording, and a step-by-step visual playback timeline when frames were captured ( artifacts.playback ). Videos up to 8 MB are inlined; larger videos are linked by a relative path, so keep them next to report.html . When to use: sharing results with teammates, reviewing visual state after a run, or archiving test evidence. ---

sections.heading: Allure
sections.text: Generates Allure result files for rich CI dashboards with history, trends, and categorized failures. Enable: --reporter allure Output: allure-results/ directory (relative to the current working directory; not configurable from the CLI or config), containing -result.json files and an environment.properties file. Run tests with Allure reporter spana test --reporter console,allure Generate and open the Allure report npx allure generate allure-results --clean -o allure-report npx allure open allure-report The reporter produces: - Result files — one JSON file per flow with UUID, history ID, labels, steps, and timing - Attachments — screenshots and hierarchy dumps copied into the output directory - Environment properties — platform, framework name, pass/fail counts - Flaky detection — tests that pass on retry are tagged as flaky with attempt count - Step mapping — spana steps (tap, assertVisible, etc.) map to Allure test steps with status and duration When to use: CI dashboards that support Allure (Jenkins Allure Plugin, GitHub Actions with allure-report action, GitLab with Allure integration). ---

sections.heading: GitHub
sections.text: Writes a Markdown run summary for GitHub Actions job summaries and pull request comments: pass/fail/skip counts, a per-platform table, and collapsible failure details with suggestions. Enable: --reporter github Output: /github-pr-summary.md (default ./spana-output/github-pr-summary.md ). When $GITHUB STEP SUMMARY is set, the same Markdown is also appended to the job summary. With --changed-since , the filter notes are included. When to use: GitHub Actions runs where you want results in the job summary, or a file to post as a PR comment. ---

sections.heading: Combining reporters
sections.text: A common setup for CI: reporters: ["console", "junit", "html"], }); This gives you live terminal feedback, a JUnit file for CI test-result ingestion, and an HTML report to upload as a build artifact. ---

sections.heading: Custom reporters
sections.text: Need a reporter that isn't built in? See Custom Reporters to learn how to write your own using spana's Reporter interface.

title: Custom Reporters
description: Extend Spana's output pipeline with your own reporter modules.

sections.text: Custom reporters let you push results into Slack, internal dashboards, CSV files, metrics systems, or any other destination.

sections.heading: Reporter shape
sections.text: Import reporter types from spana-test : const reporter: Reporter = { onFlowStart(name, platform, workerName) { console.log( START ${platform}:${workerName ?? "default"} ${name} ); }, onFlowFail(result: FlowResult) { console.log( FAIL ${result.name}: ${result.error?.message} ); }, onRunComplete(summary: RunSummary) { console.log( ${summary.passed}/${summary.total} passed ); }, }; All hooks except onRunComplete are optional. onFlowPass and onFlowFail fire for passed and failed flows; skipped flows fire neither and appear only in summary.results . Results are redacted before they reach any reporter.

sections.heading: Registering a reporter
sections.text: reporters: ["console", "./reporters/slack.ts"], }); Paths that start with . are resolved relative to the directory of spana.config.ts . Other values are imported as package names. You can also pass a module path on the CLI, for example spana test --reporter console,./reporters/slack.ts .

sections.heading: Factory reporters
sections.text: If your reporter needs options, export a factory function: return { onRunComplete(summary) { console.log( Write results into ${options.outputDir} ); }, }; } Spana calls factory reporters with { outputDir } . The value is the directory of spana.config.ts , not artifacts.outputDir .

sections.heading: Reporter
sections.text: interface Reporter { onFlowStart?(name: string, platform: Platform, workerName?: string): void; onFlowPass?(result: FlowResult): void; onFlowFail?(result: FlowResult): void; onRunComplete(summary: RunSummary): void; flowCount?: number; platformFlowCounts?: Partial ; } flowCount and platformFlowCounts are populated by Spana so console-style reporters can render progress.

sections.heading: FlowResult
sections.text: Field Description --------------- ----------------------------------------------------------- name Flow name platform web , android , ios , electron , or electrobun status passed , failed , or skipped flaky true when the flow failed first and later passed on retry attempts Number of attempts made durationMs Total runtime in milliseconds error Structured FlowError for failed flows attachments Captured artifacts such as screenshots, HAR, or logs steps Low-level driver steps recorded for the flow scenarioSteps Gherkin step results for scenario-style flows workerName Worker or device name when parallel mode is enabled

sections.heading: RunSummary
sections.text: Field Description ------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------- total Total flow executions across all platforms passed / failed / skipped Final result counts flaky Number of flaky flows durationMs Total run duration results All FlowResult entries platforms Platforms included in the run bailedOut true when --bail stopped the run early bailLimit Bail threshold that triggered the stop workerStats Per-worker timing and flow counts in parallel mode

sections.heading: StepResult and ScenarioStepResult
sections.text: StepResult represents low-level driver actions such as taps, assertions, typing, or network setup. ScenarioStepResult represents higher-level Gherkin steps such as Given , When , Then , And , But , Before , and After . Each scenario step can include nested steps for the underlying driver actions.

sections.heading: Attachment
sections.text: interface Attachment { name: string; contentType: string; path: string; } Attachments point at files on disk, for example screenshots, hierarchy dumps, console logs, JavaScript errors, or HAR captures.

sections.heading: FlowError and FailureCategory
sections.text: interface FlowError { message: string; stack?: string; category: FailureCategory; suggestion?: string; errorCode?: string; } FailureCategory values include: - element-not-found - element-not-visible - element-off-screen - element-not-interactive - text-mismatch - timeout - device-disconnected - app-crashed - app-not-installed - driver-error - config-error - unknown

sections.heading: Example: failure webhook
sections.text: Spana does not await reporter hooks, and the process exits soon after onRunComplete . An async hook like this one can be cut off before the request finishes, so keep the work small or write to disk synchronously. const reporter: Reporter = { async onFlowFail(result) { await fetch("https://hooks.example.com/test-failures", { method: "POST", headers: { "content-type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify({ name: result.name, platform: result.platform, category: result.error?.category, message: result.error?.message, worker: result.workerName, attachments: result.attachments?.map((attachment) = attachment.name), }), }); }, onRunComplete(summary) { console.log( ${summary.failed} failed flow(s) ); }, };

title: Agent API
description: Programmatic API for connecting to local web, Android, iOS, Electron, and Electrobun targets from your own scripts.

sections.text: The spana-test/agent export gives you a persistent automation session outside the flow runner. It is useful for custom scripts, AI agents, internal tooling, and live debugging.

sections.heading: Installation
sections.text: The agent API ships with spana-test .

sections.heading: Connecting
sections.text: const session = await connect({ platform: "web", baseUrl: "http://localhost:3000", headless: false, }); await session.tap({ testID: "login-button" }); await session.disconnect();

sections.heading: ConnectOptions
sections.text: interface ConnectOptions { platform: "web" "android" "ios" "electron" "electrobun"; device?: string; baseUrl?: string; browser?: "chromium" "firefox" "webkit"; headless?: boolean; storageState?: string; verboseLogging?: boolean; storybook?: { url?: string; iframePath?: string; }; packageName?: string; bundleId?: string; entry?: string; executablePath?: string; cdpUrl?: string; cdpPort?: number; renderer?: "native" "cef"; } Option Platform Description ---------------- -------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- platform all Target platform device android, ios Explicit device ID from spana devices baseUrl web Base URL to open when the browser session starts (default http://localhost:3000 ) browser web Browser engine: chromium , firefox , or webkit headless web Run the browser headless, default true storageState web Preload Playwright cookies and storage state verboseLogging web Print verbose Playwright runtime logs storybook web Storybook URL and iframe config for openStory() packageName android Android application ID bundleId ios iOS bundle identifier entry electron Electron main entry file to launch executablePath electron, electrobun App executable to launch cdpUrl electron, electrobun Attach to a running app over CDP cdpPort electron, electrobun CDP port to use renderer electrobun Electrobun renderer: native or cef Web sessions use the Playwright driver. connect() does not take a browser engine option.

title: Architecture Overview
description: High-level architecture, layered design, and element resolution flow.

sections.text: spana uses a layered architecture where all logic lives in TypeScript on the host machine. Platform drivers are thin clients (HTTP for UiAutomator2/WebDriverAgent/Appium, CDP or Playwright for browsers and desktop webviews) with no embedded selector logic.

sections.heading: High-level architecture
sections.text: graph TD A[flow files .flow.ts] -- B[CLI: spana test] B -- C[TestRunner / runner.ts] C -- D[PlatformOrchestrator] D -- E1[Web: Playwright, direct CDP, or Lightpanda] D -- E2[Android: UiAutomator2] D -- E3[iOS: WebDriverAgent] D -- E4[Electron / Electrobun] E1 -- F[Reporter] E2 -- F E3 -- F E4 -- F F -- G1[console] F -- G2[json] F -- G3[junit] F -- G4[html] F -- G5[allure / github] By default, platforms run one after another so each runtime has exclusive access to its simulator, emulator, or browser. They run concurrently when you pass --parallel , --workers , or --devices , or set parallelPlatforms: true in config. Within a platform, flows run serially on one worker, or are pulled from a shared queue when the platform has several workers (see Parallel execution). Results are collected and passed to the configured reporter(s).

sections.heading: Layered architecture
sections.text: graph TD subgraph User API A1["flow() — define test"] A2["app — launch, tap, swipe, type"] A3["expect — toBeVisible, toHaveText, toBeHidden"] end subgraph Smart Layer [Smart Layer — src/smart/] B1[coordinator.ts — action dispatch] B2[auto-wait.ts — poll until element appears] B3[element-matcher.ts — client-side tree search + centerOf] end subgraph Raw Driver [Raw Driver — src/drivers/raw-driver.ts] C[RawDriverService interface] C1[tapAtCoordinate / swipe / inputText] C2[dumpHierarchy — returns raw XML or JSON] C3[launchApp / stopApp / takeScreenshot] end subgraph Companion Drivers D1[playwright.ts / cdp-browser.ts — Playwright or direct CDP] D2[uiautomator2/driver.ts — HTTP to APK server] D3[wda/driver.ts — HTTP to XCTest runner] end subgraph Devices E1[Browser / Chromium] E2[Android emulator or device] E3[iOS simulator or device] end A2 -- B1 A3 -- B1 B1 -- B2 B2 -- C2 B2 -- B3 B3 -- B1 B1 -- C1 C -- D1 C -- D2 C -- D3 D1 -- E1 D2 -- E2 D3 -- E3 The Smart Layer resolves selectors to elements, derives center coordinates, then calls the thin RawDriver interface. The coordinate-level RawDriver methods know nothing about selectors. When a driver exposes an optional DOM channel (web drivers, or the in-app spana-bridge for webviews), the Smart Layer can resolve and act on selectors inside the page instead ( smart/channel-resolver.ts ).

sections.heading: Element resolution flow
sections.text: How app.tap({ testID: "login" }) executes end-to-end: sequenceDiagram participant Flow as flow.ts participant Coord as coordinator.ts participant Wait as auto-wait.ts participant Driver as RawDriverService participant Parser as platform parser participant Companion as companion server Flow- Coord: tap({ testID: "login" }) Coord- Wait: waitForElement(selector) loop poll until found or timeout Wait- Driver: dumpHierarchy() Driver- Companion: HTTP GET /session/:id/source Companion-- Driver: raw XML / JSON string Driver-- Wait: RawHierarchy Wait- Parser: parse(raw) - Element tree Wait- Wait: findElement(tree, { testID: "login" }) end Wait-- Coord: Element (with bounds) Coord- Coord: centerOf(element) - {x, y} Coord- Driver: tapAtCoordinate(x, y) Driver- Companion: HTTP POST /appium/gestures/click (Android) or /wda/tap (iOS) The diagram shows the native (Android/iOS) path. The parser is platform-specific (XML for Android/iOS, JSON for web) but always produces the same unified Element tree shape. On the native path, all matching logic runs client-side in TypeScript.

sections.heading: Parallel execution
sections.text: graph TD subgraph Flow Queue [Shared flow queue] Q1[flow 1] Q2[flow 2] Q3[flow 3] Q4[flow 4] Q5[flow 5] end subgraph Workers W1[Worker A — Pixel 7] W2[Worker B — Galaxy S23] W3[Worker C — iPhone 15 sim] end Q1 -- W1 Q2 -- W2 Q3 -- W3 Q4 -- W1 Q5 -- W2 W1 -- R[Aggregated Results] W2 -- R W3 -- R Workers share a single atomic index into the flow array. Because Bun is single-threaded, the increment is naturally safe with no mutex. A faster device finishes sooner and picks up the next flow immediately, draining the queue at the speed of the fastest workers. When a previous run recorded flow durations ( spana-output/.spana/last-run.json ), the queue is ordered longest-first. For web, --workers creates n isolated browser contexts spread across ceil(n / execution.web.maxContextsPerBrowser) browser processes (default: 4 multiplexed contexts per browser for the cdp engine, 2 for playwright ). Android and iOS get one worker per discovered device. - parallel.ts — runParallel() launches all workers with Promise.all , each looping over the queue until exhausted. - orchestrator.ts — orchestrate() runs each platform (single worker or runParallel() pool). Platforms run serially unless parallelPlatforms is enabled. - runtime/local.ts — buildWebRuntimePool() builds the web worker pool.

title: Drivers
description: Driver architecture — Playwright, direct CDP, UiAutomator2, WebDriverAgent, and the thin client model.

sections.text: All platform interaction in spana flows through the RawDriverService interface. Platform-specific drivers implement this interface as thin clients (HTTP for UiAutomator2 / WebDriverAgent / Appium, CDP or Playwright for browsers and desktop webviews). The core methods carry no selection logic, no auto-wait, no retry — just raw platform calls.

sections.heading: RawDriverService interface
sections.text: // Simplified — see src/drivers/raw-driver.ts for the full interface. interface RawDriverService { dumpHierarchy(): Effect.Effect ; tapAtCoordinate(x: number, y: number): Effect.Effect ; doubleTapAtCoordinate(x: number, y: number): Effect.Effect ; longPressAtCoordinate(x: number, y: number, duration: number): Effect.Effect ; swipe( startX: number, startY: number, endX: number, endY: number, duration: number, ): Effect.Effect ; inputText(text: string): Effect.Effect ; pressKey(key: string): Effect.Effect ; hideKeyboard(): Effect.Effect ; takeScreenshot(): Effect.Effect ; getDeviceInfo(): Effect.Effect ; launchApp(bundleId: string, opts?: LaunchOptions): Effect.Effect ; stopApp(bundleId: string): Effect.Effect ; killApp(bundleId: string): Effect.Effect ; clearAppState(bundleId: string): Effect.Effect ; openLink(url: string): Effect.Effect ; back(): Effect.Effect ; evaluate ( script: string ((...args: any[]) = T), ...args: unknown[] ): Effect.Effect ; // Optional capabilities (present only on drivers that support them): // pinch / zoom / multiTouch, webview contexts, domChannel, network mocking, // cookies / auth state, tabs, console logs / JS errors / HAR, WebAuthn virtual authenticator. domChannel?: DomChannel; } The Smart Layer ( coordinator.ts , auto-wait.ts , element-matcher.ts , channel-resolver.ts ) is the main consumer of this interface. Flow authors do not normally use it directly (the debug REPL exposes it as driver ). The optional domChannel is the one place selectors reach a driver: web drivers and the in-app spana-bridge use it to resolve and act on elements inside the page.

sections.heading: Web drivers (Playwright, direct CDP, Lightpanda)
sections.text: The web engine is selected with execution.web.engine ( resolveWebEngine() in src/runtime/local.ts ): Engine Driver Notes ------------------------ ---------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- "playwright" (default) src/drivers/playwright.ts Uses playwright-core . Supports chromium , firefox , webkit , channel , wsEndpoint , and HAR recording. "cdp" src/drivers/cdp-browser.ts Launches Chromium itself (or attaches to execution.web.cdpUrl ) and talks to it over a raw CDP WebSocket, with no Playwright client. Auto-attaches to cross-origin (out-of-process) iframes. "lightpanda" src/drivers/cdp-browser.ts Connects over CDP to an already-running Lightpanda server at execution.web.cdpUrl (default http://127.0.0.1:9222 ). spana does not start Lightpanda. "auto" — Picks "cdp" when the browser is Chromium and none of wsEndpoint , channel , or artifacts.har is set; otherwise "playwright" . - The playwright and cdp engines launch the browser (or attach to cdpUrl / wsEndpoint ); all engines navigate to apps.web.url (default http://localhost:3000 ) and expose the page via the RawDriverService interface. - dumpHierarchy() walks the DOM inside the page ( page.evaluate on Playwright, Runtime.evaluate on CDP) and returns it as structured JSON. - Coordinate taps are issued via page.mouse.click(x, y) on Playwright and Input.dispatchMouseEvent on CDP. - Both drivers expose a DOM channel, so the Smart Layer can resolve selectors inside the page. Desktop targets use the same web parser: Electron ( src/drivers/electron.ts , Playwright electron or CDP attach) and Electrobun ( src/drivers/electrobun.ts , CDP or WebKit inspector).

sections.heading: Android driver (UiAutomator2)
sections.text: The Android driver is a pure HTTP client that talks to the UiAutomator2 APK server running on the device. Setup sequence ( src/drivers/uiautomator2/installer.ts ): 1. spana installs the UiAutomator2 server and test APKs via ADB if they are not already on the device. The APKs come from the optional appium-uiautomator2-server dependency (or a local drivers/android/ directory). 2. It starts the server on the device with adb shell am instrument (port 6790). 3. ADB port-forwarding maps device port 6790 to a local port (allocated from 8200). 4. The driver sends HTTP requests to http://localhost: . With execution.warmDaemons.enabled , a healthy server from an earlier run is reused instead. Key endpoints (all under /session/:id ): - GET /source — returns the full UI hierarchy as XML - POST /appium/gestures/click — taps at coordinates - POST /appium/device/activate app — launches the app by package name The driver parses the XML hierarchy in TypeScript and produces the unified Element tree. No XML parsing happens in the APK.

sections.heading: iOS driver (WebDriverAgent)
sections.text: The iOS driver is a pure HTTP client that talks to the WebDriverAgent (WDA) XCTest bundle running on the simulator or device. spana finds the WDA Xcode project in the optional appium-webdriveragent dependency (or a local drivers/ios/WebDriverAgent/ directory) and builds it with xcodebuild ( src/drivers/wda/installer.ts ). Simulator setup: 1. On first use for a simulator, spana runs xcodebuild build-for-testing without code signing and caches the build in .wda-builds/ . 2. It starts WDA with xcodebuild test-without-building on a port allocated from 8100. 3. The driver sends HTTP requests to http://localhost: . Device setup: 1. With apps.ios.signing.teamId set, spana builds WDA for the device with DEVELOPMENT TEAM and CODE SIGN IDENTITY (default "Apple Development" ), then starts it. 2. iproxy (from libimobiledevice ) forwards the device port to a local port. 3. The driver connects to the forwarded port. Without signing , spana assumes WDA is already running on the device and only opens the iproxy tunnel. Key endpoints (all under /session/:id ): - GET /source — returns the full accessibility tree as XML - POST /wda/tap — taps at coordinates - POST /wda/apps/launch — launches the app by bundle ID

sections.heading: Hierarchy parsing
sections.text: Each platform returns a different hierarchy format: Platform Format Parser location --------------------------- ------------------------------- ---------------------------------------- Android XML (UiAutomator ViewHierarchy) src/drivers/uiautomator2/pagesource.ts iOS XML (WDA accessibility tree) src/drivers/wda/pagesource.ts Web / Electron / Electrobun JSON (in-page DOM walk) src/drivers/playwright-parser.ts All parsers output the same unified Element type: // Simplified from src/schemas/element.ts interface Element { id?: string; // testID / resource-id / accessibility identifier text?: string; value?: string; accessibilityLabel?: string; resourceId?: string; elementType?: string; bounds: { x: number; y: number; width: number; height: number }; enabled?: boolean; visible?: boolean; clickable?: boolean; focused?: boolean; attributes?: Record ; children?: Element[]; } element-matcher.ts in the Smart Layer searches this tree for the selector — no platform-specific code required.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The thin HTTP client approach used by the WDA and UiAutomator2 drivers was inspired by maestro-runner, a Go project that demonstrated how minimal HTTP clients can effectively drive device interaction without heavy abstractions. The web drivers follow a similar philosophy: the cdp engine speaks raw CDP over a WebSocket, and the playwright engine calls Playwright directly rather than wrapping it in additional layers.

title: Device Setup
description: Set up Android emulators, iOS simulators, and physical devices for testing.

sections.text: Spana auto-discovers available devices for each platform. This guide covers how to set up and verify your devices before running tests.

sections.heading: Checking available devices
sections.text: spana devices This lists discovered devices for all platforms (web, Electron, Electrobun, Android, iOS) as platform, name, type, and state: web Chromium (Playwright) browser available electron Electron (Playwright electron / CDP) desktop available electrobun Electrobun (Native WebView / CEF) desktop available android emulator-5554 emulator device ios iPhone 16 (iOS.18.4) simulator Booted ios iPhone 16 Pro (iOS.18.4) simulator Shutdown For Android, the name is the serial you pass to --device . The plain output does not show iOS UDIDs: use spana devices --json to get each device's id .

sections.heading: Web
sections.text: Web testing uses a local Chromium by default. Install a Playwright browser once ( npx playwright install chromium ), or point execution.web.executablePath (or execution.web.channel on the playwright engine) at an installed browser. The cdp engine falls back to a system Chrome when no Playwright Chromium is found. spana doctor checks this for you. Spana always shows playwright-chromium as an available web device. The browser engine ( execution.web.engine : "playwright" default, "cdp" , "lightpanda" , or "auto" ) is chosen in config, not by device.

sections.heading: Android
sections.text: Spana discovers Android devices through adb (Android Debug Bridge).

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text: - Android SDK -- install via Android Studio or the command-line tools - ADB -- included in the Android SDK platform tools - Java 17+ -- required by UiAutomator2

sections.heading: Using an emulator
sections.text: In a single-device run (no --parallel / --workers / --devices ), if no device or emulator is connected, spana boots the first AVD from emulator -list-avds for you. To start one yourself: List available AVDs emulator -list-avds Start an emulator emulator -avd Pixel 7 API 34 & Verify it appears adb devices emulator-5554 device

sections.heading: Using a physical device
sections.text: 1. Enable Developer Options on the device 2. Enable USB Debugging in Developer Options 3. Connect via USB and accept the debugging prompt 4. Verify: adb devices should show your device serial

sections.heading: Targeting a specific device
sections.text: When multiple Android devices are connected: Use the --device flag with the serial from spana devices spana test --platform android --device emulator-5554

sections.heading: iOS
sections.text: Spana discovers iOS simulators through Xcode's simctl (all available simulators, booted or not) and connected physical devices through xcrun devicectl (Xcode 15+). When you do not pass --device , spana tries a connected physical device first and falls back to a simulator. It prefers a simulator that already has your app installed (booted first), then any booted simulator, then the first available one, and boots it if needed. Boot a simulator before you target it with --device .

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text: - Xcode -- install from the Mac App Store - Xcode Command Line Tools -- xcode-select --install - WebDriverAgent -- spana builds it with xcodebuild from the optional appium-webdriveragent dependency on first use per simulator

sections.heading: Booting a simulator
sections.text: List all available simulators xcrun simctl list devices available Boot a simulator xcrun simctl boot "iPhone 16" Or open the Simulator app open -a Simulator

sections.heading: Targeting a specific simulator
sections.text: Use the UDID from spana devices --json spana test --platform ios --device 7338EC82-D2BD-4722-B148-D009FDA64F6E

sections.heading: Physical iOS devices
sections.text: Physical iOS devices need iproxy ( brew install libimobiledevice ) and a signed WebDriverAgent. Add your team ID so spana can build and sign WDA for the device: title="spana.config.ts" apps: { ios: { bundleId: "com.example.myapp", signing: { teamId: "YOUR TEAM ID", signingIdentity: "Apple Development", // optional, this is the default }, }, }, }); signing accepts only teamId and signingIdentity . Without signing , spana expects WebDriverAgent to already be running on the device and only opens the iproxy tunnel.

sections.heading: Multi-device testing
sections.text: Run the same flows on multiple devices simultaneously. --device takes a single ID; use --devices (comma-separated) or --parallel for more than one: Run on a specific Android and iOS device spana test --devices emulator-5554,7338EC82-D2BD-4722-B148-D009FDA64F6E Auto-discover all devices and run in parallel (cap with --workers ) spana test --platform android,ios --parallel With --devices , platforms are inferred from the selected devices when --platform is not set. --devices cannot be combined with --device . When none of --device , --devices , --parallel , or --workers is provided, spana uses one device per platform, chosen as described above.

sections.heading: Android: "no devices found"
sections.text: - Check adb devices shows your device with state device (not offline or unauthorized ) - Restart ADB: adb kill-server && adb start-server - For emulators, ensure the emulator is fully booted (wait for the home screen)

sections.heading: iOS: "No iOS simulator or physical device available"
sections.text: - Check that at least one simulator is available: xcrun simctl list devices available - If none is listed, create one in Xcode (Settings Platforms / Devices and Simulators) - To skip the boot wait, boot one first: xcrun simctl boot "iPhone 16"

sections.heading: iOS: WebDriverAgent build fails
sections.text: - Check that appium-webdriveragent is installed (it is an optional dependency), or place WDA in drivers/ios/WebDriverAgent/ - Open WebDriverAgent.xcodeproj in Xcode and resolve signing issues - Ensure your Xcode version matches the simulator runtime - Try: xcodebuild -showsdks to verify available SDKs

title: Remote Execution
description: Run tests against remote Appium servers and cloud device farms.

sections.text: By default, spana runs tests locally using built-in drivers (Playwright or direct CDP for web, UiAutomator2 for Android, WebDriverAgent for iOS). Switch to Appium mode to run Android and iOS against a remote Appium server — useful for cloud device farms, shared test infrastructure, or devices on another machine. Web, Electron, and Electrobun still run locally in Appium mode.

sections.heading: Config file
sections.text: title="spana.config.ts" execution: { mode: "appium", appium: { serverUrl: "http://localhost:4723", }, }, });

sections.heading: CLI flags
sections.text: spana test --appium-url http://localhost:4723 The --appium-url flag automatically enables Appium mode. You can also select the mode explicitly with --driver appium (or --driver local to override a config that sets mode: "appium" ). The server URL is resolved in this order: --appium-url , the SPANA APPIUM URL environment variable, then execution.appium.serverUrl . SPANA APPIUM URL only supplies the URL; it does not switch on Appium mode by itself.

sections.heading: Auto-starting a local Appium server
sections.text: With --appium-auto-start (or execution.appium.autoStart: true ), spana spawns appium from PATH for the duration of the run and ignores any configured URL. Appium mode must still be on ( mode: "appium" or --driver appium ). Use autoStartBinary and autoStartArgs to change the binary or pass extra arguments.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: In Appium mode, spana: 1. Connects to the Appium server at the given URL 2. Creates one session per platform with the resolved capabilities 3. Runs your flows using the Appium WebDriver protocol instead of local drivers 4. Deletes the session when the run completes 5. Reports results to the cloud provider if detected The same flow files work in both local and Appium mode -- no changes needed. Appium mode runs one session per platform. --parallel , --workers , and --devices use the local device-discovery path and do not create Appium sessions.

sections.heading: Cloud helper config
sections.text: For BrowserStack and Sauce Labs, Spana can also manage provider-specific helper behavior on top of raw capabilities: - upload a local app artifact and inject appium:app - start and stop BrowserStack Local / Sauce Connect - fill missing bstack:options / sauce:options values from config Raw capabilities still win. Helper config fills missing provider fields and lifecycle, but it does not override explicit appium:app , bstack:options , or sauce:options values you already provided through config, --caps , or --caps-json .

sections.heading: Capabilities
sections.text: Appium sessions are configured through W3C capabilities. Spana merges capabilities from five sources (later overrides earlier): Source How to set Example ------------------- -------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------- Launch device state launchOptions.deviceState { language: "sv", locale: "sv SE" } Config file execution.appium.capabilities { "appium:app": "/path/to/app" } Platform config execution.appium.platformCapabilities.android / .ios { "appium:deviceName": "iPhone 15" } JSON file --caps or capabilitiesFile in config caps.json Inline CLI --caps-json ' ' '{"appium:deviceName": "Pixel 7"}'

sections.heading: Android capabilities
sections.text: title="caps-android.json" { "appium:automationName": "UiAutomator2", "appium:deviceName": "emulator-5554", "appium:app": "/path/to/app.apk", "appium:appPackage": "com.example.myapp", "appium:appActivity": "com.example.myapp.MainActivity" } Spana sets platformName: "Android" by default. Your capabilities can override it.

sections.heading: iOS capabilities
sections.text: title="caps-ios.json" { "appium:automationName": "XCUITest", "appium:deviceName": "iPhone 15", "appium:platformVersion": "18.0", "appium:app": "/path/to/app.ipa", "appium:bundleId": "com.example.myapp" } Spana sets platformName: "iOS" and appium:automationName: "XCUITest" by default. Your capabilities can override them.

sections.heading: Local Appium server
sections.text: To test against a local Appium server: Install Appium npm install -g appium Install drivers appium driver install uiautomator2 appium driver install xcuitest Start the server appium Run tests against it spana test --appium-url http://localhost:4723

sections.heading: Config reference
sections.text: title="spana.config.ts" execution: { mode: "appium", appium: { // Appium server URL (required in appium mode) serverUrl: "http://localhost:4723", // Inline capabilities (applied after launchOptions.deviceState) capabilities: { "appium:app": "/path/to/app.apk", }, // Per-platform capabilities (override capabilities ) platformCapabilities: { android: { "appium:deviceName": "Pixel 7" }, ios: { "appium:deviceName": "iPhone 15" }, }, // Path to a JSON capabilities file, resolved relative to spana.config.ts // (overrides config capabilities; --caps-json overrides this) capabilitiesFile: "./caps.json", // Report results to cloud provider (default: true) reportToProvider: true, // Spawn a local appium for the run (default: false) autoStart: false, autoStartBinary: "appium", autoStartArgs: [], // Custom cloud provider module (see Cloud Providers guide) // cloudProvider: "./providers/acme-grid.ts", // BrowserStack helper config browserstack: { app: { path: "./builds/app.apk", customId: "spana-android" }, local: { enabled: true, identifier: "spana-local" }, options: { projectName: "my-app", buildName: "ci-42", }, }, // Sauce Labs helper config saucelabs: { app: { path: "./builds/app.apk", name: "app.apk" }, connect: { enabled: true, tunnelName: "spana-ci" }, options: { build: "ci-42", name: "login-flow", }, }, }, }, });

sections.heading: CLI flags
sections.text: Flag Description -------------------------- --------------------------------------- --appium-url Appium server URL (enables appium mode) --driver Select the execution mode explicitly --appium-auto-start Spawn a local appium for the run --caps Path to capabilities JSON file --caps-json Inline capabilities JSON string --no-provider-reporting Disable cloud provider result reporting

sections.heading: Cloud providers
sections.text: When the Appium URL points to BrowserStack or Sauce Labs, spana auto-detects the provider and reports test results. See the Cloud Providers guide for setup details.

title: Cloud Providers
description: Run tests on BrowserStack and Sauce Labs device clouds.

sections.text: Spana can run mobile (Android and iOS) tests on cloud device farms through Appium. It auto-detects BrowserStack and Sauce Labs from the server URL hostname, reports the run result back to the provider dashboard, and can manage provider-specific upload/tunnel helpers from config. Keep the credentials in the URL ( https://USER:KEY@... ): managed uploads, tunnels, and result reporting read them from there.

sections.heading: Supported providers
sections.text: Provider Auto-detected Result reporting Managed helpers --------------------------------- ------------- ---------------- ------------------------- BrowserStack Yes Yes Yes Sauce Labs Yes Yes Yes Custom provider ( cloudProvider ) -- No (see below) Yes (your createHelper ) Other Appium grid -- No No

sections.heading: 1. Set your credentials
sections.text: Embed credentials in the Appium server URL: title="spana.config.ts" execution: { mode: "appium", appium: { serverUrl: "https://USER:KEY@hub-cloud.browserstack.com/wd/hub", }, }, }); Or pass them on the CLI: spana test --appium-url "https://USER:KEY@hub-cloud.browserstack.com/wd/hub"

sections.heading: 2. Set capabilities or helper config
sections.text: Create a caps.json file with BrowserStack-specific options: title="caps.json" { "bstack:options": { "projectName": "my-app", "buildName": "ci-42", "deviceName": "Samsung Galaxy S23", "os version": "13.0" }, "appium:app": "bs://app-id-from-upload" } Then reference it: spana test --caps caps.json Or let Spana manage app upload, BrowserStack Local, and default bstack:options values from config: title="spana.config.ts" apps: { android: { packageName: "com.example.myapp", appPath: "./builds/app.apk", }, }, execution: { mode: "appium", appium: { serverUrl: "https://USER:KEY@hub-cloud.browserstack.com/wd/hub", browserstack: { app: { customId: "spana-android", }, local: { enabled: true, identifier: "spana-local", }, options: { projectName: "my-app", buildName: process.env.CI BUILD ID ?? "local", }, }, capabilities: { "appium:deviceName": "Samsung Galaxy S23", "appium:platformVersion": "13.0", }, }, }, }); When an execution.appium.browserstack block is present, Spana uploads browserstack.app.path , or apps. .appPath when that is not set, and injects the returned bs://... URL as appium:app . Use browserstack.app.id when you already have a bs://... reference. If appium:app or bstack:options are already set in raw capabilities, those explicit values win and helper config only fills what is missing.

sections.heading: 3. Result reporting
sections.text: Spana reports pass/fail status to BrowserStack once, after the whole run completes. This updates each Appium session in the BrowserStack dashboard with the name spana and passed (no flow failed) or failed . No per-flow status or failure reason is sent. Disable reporting with --no-provider-reporting or in config: appium: { reportToProvider: false, } When browserstack.local.enabled is true, Spana starts and stops BrowserStack Local for the run. Set browserstack.local.binary if the BrowserStackLocal binary is not on PATH , or keep managing the tunnel yourself and pass bstack:options.local manually.

sections.heading: 1. Set your credentials
sections.text: title="spana.config.ts" execution: { mode: "appium", appium: { serverUrl: "https://USER:KEY@ondemand.us-west-1.saucelabs.com/wd/hub", }, }, }); For EU data center: spana test --appium-url "https://USER:KEY@ondemand.eu-central-1.saucelabs.com/wd/hub"

sections.heading: 2. Set capabilities or helper config
sections.text: title="caps.json" { "sauce:options": { "name": "login-flow", "build": "ci-42", "appiumVersion": "2.0" }, "appium:deviceName": "Google Pixel 7", "appium:platformVersion": "13", "appium:app": "storage:filename=app.apk" } Or let Spana manage Sauce storage uploads, Sauce Connect, and default sauce:options values from config: title="spana.config.ts" apps: { android: { packageName: "com.example.myapp", appPath: "./builds/app.apk", }, }, execution: { mode: "appium", appium: { serverUrl: "https://USER:KEY@ondemand.us-west-1.saucelabs.com/wd/hub", saucelabs: { app: { name: "app.apk", }, connect: { enabled: true, tunnelName: "spana-ci", }, options: { build: process.env.CI BUILD ID ?? "local", name: "login-flow", }, }, capabilities: { "appium:deviceName": "Google Pixel 7", "appium:platformVersion": "13", }, }, }, }); When an execution.appium.saucelabs block is present, Spana uploads saucelabs.app.path , or apps. .appPath when that is not set, to Sauce storage and injects storage: as appium:app . Use saucelabs.app.id when you already have a Sauce storage reference such as storage:YOUR APP ID . Explicit appium:app and sauce:options capability values still override helper-derived defaults.

sections.heading: 3. Result reporting
sections.text: Sauce Labs sessions are updated with pass/fail status once, after the whole run completes (same rules as BrowserStack). Region is detected from the server URL hostname: uploads and Sauce Connect use eu-central , us-east , or us-west (default); result reporting uses eu-central-1 when the hostname contains eu-central , otherwise us-west-1 . When saucelabs.connect.enabled is true, Spana starts and stops Sauce Connect for the run. Set saucelabs.connect.binary if the sc binary is not on PATH , or keep managing the tunnel yourself and pass sauce:options.tunnelName manually.

sections.heading: Capability resolution
sections.text: Capabilities merge from five sources, with later sources overriding earlier ones ( src/runtime/capabilities.ts ): 1. Launch device state -- launchOptions.deviceState ( language / locale / timeZone ) mapped to Appium capabilities 2. Config file -- execution.appium.capabilities in spana.config.ts 3. Platform-specific config -- execution.appium.platformCapabilities.android or .ios , for the platform being run 4. Capabilities file -- --caps flag or execution.appium.capabilitiesFile in config 5. Inline CLI JSON -- --caps-json '{"key": "value"}' This lets you keep shared capabilities in config, platform or environment-specific ones in platformCapabilities or a file, and override individual values from the CLI. Cloud helper config is applied after this merge and only fills fields that are still missing.

sections.heading: Custom cloud providers
sections.text: If you use an Appium grid other than BrowserStack or Sauce Labs, point execution.appium.cloudProvider at a module that default-exports a CloudProvider . title="spana.config.ts" execution: { mode: "appium", appium: { serverUrl: "https://grid.example.com/wd/hub", cloudProvider: "./providers/acme-grid.ts", }, }, }); The module path is resolved relative to spana.config.ts . :::caution Today the CLI only calls createHelper() (and the helper's prepareCapabilities() / cleanup() ) on a custom provider. End-of-run result reporting is only wired for the built-in BrowserStack and Sauce Labs providers, so a custom extractMeta() / reportResult() is not called by spana test . :::

sections.heading: CloudProvider
sections.text: const provider: CloudProvider = { name() { return "Acme Grid"; }, createHelper(appiumUrl, config): CloudProviderHelper { return { async prepareCapabilities(platform, caps, appConfig) { return { ...caps, "acme:options": { platform, appIdentifier: appConfig?.packageName ?? appConfig?.bundleId, }, }; }, async cleanup() { // stop tunnels, delete temporary uploads, etc. }, }; }, extractMeta(sessionId, caps, meta) { meta.sessionId = sessionId; meta.build = String(caps["build"] ?? ""); }, async reportResult(appiumUrl, meta, result) { await fetch( ${appiumUrl}/custom-results/${meta.sessionId} , { method: "POST", headers: { "content-type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify(result), }); }, };

sections.heading: Interface responsibilities
sections.text: API Responsibility ----------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- name() Human-readable provider name createHelper() Build a helper for capability mutation and lifecycle cleanup prepareCapabilities() Add provider-specific desired capabilities before session creation cleanup() Tear down uploads, tunnels, or temporary state after the run extractMeta() Pull provider metadata from the created session for reporting (built-in providers only today) reportResult() Mark the remote session passed or failed (built-in providers only today)
